title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR scoring rule, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate was generated per paired intent and the same candidate was replayed to both arms (baseline is therefore not an independent-generation condition). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared candidate). Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, this study quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) offer a practical route to automate intent-driven network configuration, yet operators reasonably fear that automatically generated configurations can enlarge attack surface, violate access-control policies, or introduce other security-relevant regressions. Systems work and surveys therefore recommend constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational mitigations. Prior reports show GVR-like architectures can improve correctness for code and IaC tasks, but rigorous, preregistered confirmation that verifier insertion reduces forbidden-reachability misconfigurations under adversarial inputs remains limited for NetOps-specific, execution-validated pipelines.

We designed, preregistered, and executed a paired experiment to answer a narrowly scoped operational question: under a fixed adapter contract and a deterministic execution substrate, does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? The design intentionally fixes key axes (paired sampling, shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, declared model, deterministic validators, Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation) so that the run provides a clean, auditable test of whether verifier insertion changes the observed safety outcome for the chosen configuration of model, validators, and intent set. The experiment produced a degenerate but informative confirmatory outcome: every sampled intent produced a configuration that passed the forbidden-reachability predicate in both arms (n11 = 300), so the repair path was never exercised. We report the preregistered design, deterministic execution evidence, exact quantitative outcomes, and consequence-driven recommendations for follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths.
sections.related_work:
Three converging literatures informed our design and interpretation. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have demonstrated substantive gains on code and Infrastructure-as-Code benchmarks by using verifier feedback to direct corrective generations; reported systems show that realized gains depend strongly on verifier expressiveness and repair strategy (e.g., TerraFormer and related work showing verifier-guided improvements on policy-guided IaC) [verified records]. Second, NetOps and LLM-in-operations surveys document recurring LLM failure modes—hallucination, calibration errors, and domain mismatch—and widely recommend integrating validators, constrained decoding, or human oversight to reduce operational risk; these surveys also note that emulation-based evaluations are common but can fail to capture production device heterogeneity. Third, emulation and testbed work demonstrates that execution-based validation of generated network artifacts is feasible in research settings (Dockerized FRRouting-style environments, containerized Batfish-like validators, and lightweight static analyzers are commonly used), while emphasizing external-validity limits when porting results to production.

Existing studies rarely combine (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory design, (2) deterministic validators and seeds for exact accounting, and (3) archived per-episode validator traces focused explicitly on security-relevant reachability predicates. Our study occupies that niche and is therefore primarily an evidence-centered probe of the joint effect of generation semantics, verifier presence, and deterministic adversarial perturbations under a fixed model and validator set.
sections.methodology:
Design and estimand: The preregistration fixed a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in the proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The prespecified confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two-sided test at α = 0.05; confidence intervals were to be obtained by a paired bootstrap-percentile procedure. Sensitivity checks treating technical failures as violations were prespecified; no technical failures occurred.

Adapter contract and generation semantics: To bound provider-call cost while preserving deterministic accounting, the preregistration specified shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each matched intent pair a single LLM candidate is generated and replayed to both arms (baseline = replay; guarded = same candidate validated by deterministic validators, with an allowed single repair call if validators report forbidden reachability). This contract reduces hosted-model calls to one per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) at the cost of removing independent-sample variability between arms. The preregistered trade-off is explicit: shared_initial_candidate conserves model budget but reduces the chance of observing cross-condition discordant outcomes that would allow the repair path to demonstrate efficacy.

Validators, scoring, and determinism: The preregistered validator set consisted of two deterministic validators run inside Dockerized containers: a containerized execution-style reachability validator (emulation-based executor) and a lightweight static reachability analyzer. Their outputs were combined with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair is labeled violating if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate. All seeds, orchestration parameters, and emulator images were fixed to ensure deterministic replay. Per-episode validator judgments and repair_applied flags were archived for audit.

Intervention and repair policy: Baseline is replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded is the same candidate validated by the deterministic validators and, if any validator detects forbidden reachability, the preregistered repair policy permits up to one repair LLM call per pair. Repair attempts were therefore contingent on a validator-detected violation and were not to be used proactively.

Execution contract and model declaration: The declared model in the execution manifest was gpt-5-mini. The orchestration adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1, planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), maximum_model_calls = 600, and the actual model call audit recorded model_calls_used = 300 under the shared_initial_candidate semantics. All orchestration, task generation, and scoring components were deterministic and archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed the planned episodes = 600 with completed_episode_count = 600 and failed_episode_count = 0. Provider-call accounting recorded model_calls_used = 300 (shared-initial generation per pair) and no retries or transient API failures.

Primary confirmatory outcome: Every initial candidate in the matched sample satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate under both arms: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). The paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The prespecified bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (analysis used 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729; preregistration planned 1,000 resamples but the final analysis used 10,000 to reduce Monte Carlo error) is [0.0, 0.0].

Degenerate contingency and descriptive bound: The complete absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) renders the McNemar test uninformative for repair efficacy: there were no candidate violations for the guarded condition to correct. This degenerate contingency is a direct product of (a) shared_initial_candidate semantics (reducing independent variability across arms) and (b) the observed baseline compliance (none of the adversarial variants produced a validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators). As a descriptive constraint, observing 0 violations in N = 300 independent episodes implies a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%).

Repair activity and validator concordance: Because no validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, the repair path was never invoked and all per-episode repair_applied flags are false. Validator judgments (as archived) are concordant for every episode under the logical-OR scoring rule for this run. Representative per-episode traces and the analysis artifact set (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json) are archived to support these facts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation within the execution contract: Under the exact preregistered contract—declared model gpt-5-mini, shared_initial_candidate semantics, the evaluated deterministic validator set combined by logical OR, and the synthetic intent set including programmatic adversarial variants—the LLM-generated initial candidates satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every sampled intent. Consequently, inserting a verifier into the pipeline did not change observed compliance on the sampled tasks because there were no validator-detected violations to correct. This is a valid, artifact-grounded empirical statement about the joint behavior of the chosen model, validators, and intent set under deterministic execution.

What the evidence does not show: The result does not demonstrate that verifiers are ineffective in general, nor does it show that verifier-guided repair cannot rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the degenerate observed contingency violates that assumption and makes the confirmatory McNemar inference moot with respect to repair efficacy. Thus, the experiment answers a narrowly scoped question (does verifier insertion change the observed pass rate under this contract?) rather than the broader operational question of whether verifiers can reduce security-relevant misconfigurations in general.

Design lessons for follow-up stress tests (evidence-grounded):
- Generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate materially reduces model-call overhead but also suppresses independent-sample variability between arms. For experiments intended to exercise repair efficacy, independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or enlarging the repair-call budget would increase the probability of observing discordant failures repair could address.
- Adversary potency: The programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable violations for the chosen model and validators. Follow-up studies should use stronger, targeted adversaries crafted to exploit specific verifier predicates or to induce configuration patterns near decision boundaries.
- Verifier strength and diversity: This run evaluated two deterministic validators combined by logical OR. Broader oracle diversity (stronger execution oracles, more expressive policy specifications, richer static analyzers) may detect different failure modes and thereby exercise repair paths more often.
- Operational accounting: Deterministic execution with fixed seeds and archived per-episode validator traces provides practical auditability of provider-call budgets and paired contingencies; this traceability facilitated exact reconciliation that showed model_calls_used = 300 and no repair activity.

Limitations and threats to validity (artifact-grounded): Internal validity is limited by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope. Construct validity depends on whether the chosen forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately capture operational security risk. External validity is constrained because tasks were synthetic and executed in deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; results may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic, or other operational constraints. Conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and the preregistered power assumptions are unmet. These limitations motivate carefully targeted follow-up tests rather than reinterpretation of the present confirmatory outcome.

Operational implications: For operators and researchers aiming to demonstrate or operationalize verifier-in-the-loop GVR for security-critical NetOps tasks, the decisive factors are (a) generation semantics (shared vs independent draws), (b) adversary design and potency, (c) repair budget allocation, and (d) verifier expressiveness and coverage. Experimental evidence that verifiers materially reduce security risk requires testbeds and adversaries that produce validator-detectable violations with nonnegligible frequency under baseline generation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation (declared model gpt-5-mini) with two deterministic validators combined by logical OR under a shared_initial_candidate contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate confirmatory outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Validators never reported forbidden reachability and therefore no repair calls were made; as a result, the experiment cannot assess whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violating outputs. The observed contingency implies a descriptive one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. The study highlights that experimental contracts, adversary potency, repair budgets, verifier strength, and model diversity jointly determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We archive the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to inform follow-up stress tests designed to intentionally exercise repair paths.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in the evidence bundle for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in deterministic FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
